In [[mathematics]], '''additive K-theory''' means some version of [[algebraic K-theory]] in which, according to [[Spencer Bloch]], the [[general linear group]] ''GL'' has everywhere been replaced by its [[Lie algebra]] ''gl''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bloch |first=Spencer |date=2006-07-23 |title=Algebraic Cycles and Additive Chow Groups |url=http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~bloch/addchow_rept.pdf  |publisher=Dept. of Mathematics, University of Chicago}}</ref> It is not, therefore, one theory but a way of creating additive or infinitesimal analogues of multiplicative theories.

==Formulation==

Following [[Boris Feigin]] and [[Boris Tsygan]],<ref>B. Feigin, B. Tsygan. ''Additive K-theory'', LNM 1289, Springer</ref> let <math> A </math> be an algebra over a field <math> k </math> of [[characteristic zero]] and let <math> {\mathfrak gl}(A) </math> be the algebra of infinite matrices over <math>A</math> with only finitely many nonzero entries. Then the [[Lie algebra homology]]

:<math> H_\cdot ({\mathfrak gl}(A),k) </math>

has a natural structure of a [[Hopf algebra]]. The space of its [[Primitive element (co-algebra)|primitive elements]] of degree <math> i</math> is denoted by <math>K^+_i(A)</math> and called the <math>i</math>-th '''additive K-functor''' of&nbsp;''A''.

The additive K-functors are related to [[cyclic homology]] groups by the isomorphism

:<math> HC_i(A) \cong K^+_{i+1}(A). </math>
